## Case study: *Araptus attenuatus*

The same analysis applies to field data, with two additions that real
samples need: tests are run within each connected component, against a
hypothesis of direction stated in advance, and the directional isolation
comparison is calibrated for the sampling design.

Garrick et al. (2013) inferred two range expansions of the peninsular lineage
of the bark beetle *Araptus attenuatus* out of a Pleistocene refugium near
27.5°N on the Baja California peninsula: a central group of populations
expanding south and a northern group expanding north.  If so, populations near
the refugium should read as sources and those farther from it as sinks, and
genetic distance should accumulate more slowly moving away from the refugium
than toward it.

### One graph, several components

The Population Graph is estimated from all peninsular sites with at least four
beetles; `decorate = TRUE` adds each site's mean coordinates to its node.

```{r arapat-graph}
#| cache: true
#| warning: false
data( arapat )

peninsula <- arapat |>
  filter( Species == "Peninsula" ) |>
  group_by( Population ) |>
  filter( n() >= 4 ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  droplevels()

beetles <- peninsula |>
  population_graph( decorate = TRUE )

beetles

igraph::components( beetles )$csize
```

The components recapitulate the regional populations of Garrick et al.
(2013): a central group, a northern group, and two southern dyads, which carry
no directional information.  At the degree-neutral bandwidth, the gravity field
drawn on the sites' coordinates shows the source-sink surface of each
component separately; because $S$ sums to zero within a component, colours are
comparable only within one.  A grey outline of the land from Natural Earth
(`rnaturalearth`), passed as `base =`, goes underneath, and `clip_to_base`
keeps the surface on land; the Visualization
chapter (@sec-visualization) builds a fuller base map with labels and a north
arrow.

```{r arapat-field}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
#| message: false
coords <- peninsula |>
  strata_coordinates()

land <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries( country = "Mexico",
                                     scale = "medium",
                                     returnclass = "sf" )

land_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf( data = land,
           fill = "grey92",
           colour = "grey55",
           linewidth = 0.3 ) +
  coord_sf( xlim = c( -115.5, -108.5 ),
            ylim = c( 22.5, 30 ) ) +
  labs( x = NULL, y = NULL ) +
  theme_minimal()

beetles |>
  gravity_field() |>
  plot( layout = coords,
        base = land_map,
        clip_to_base = TRUE,
        mask_dist = 0.6 )
```

### The axis: distance from the refugium

Position along the peninsula is the first principal axis of the site
coordinates (in km), and each site's distance from the refugium, $d_i$, is
measured along it.  A pair of sites is *forward* when $j$ lies farther from the
refugium than $i$.

```{r arapat-axis}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: arapat-graph
nodes <- igraph::V( beetles )$name
lon   <- igraph::V( beetles )$Longitude
lat   <- igraph::V( beetles )$Latitude
xy    <- cbind( x = lon * 111.32 * cos( mean( lat ) * pi / 180 ),
                y = lat * 110.57 )
axis  <- prcomp( xy )
v     <- axis$rotation[, 1] * sign( axis$rotation["y", 1] )
along <- setNames( as.vector( sweep( xy, 2, axis$center ) %*% v ), nodes )
refugium <- ( 27.5 * 110.57 - axis$center["y"] ) / v["y"]
d        <- abs( along - refugium )
```

### Testing each expansion within its component

A small helper runs both tests on one component: the source-sink gradient
test with $d$ as the covariate, and the directional isolation comparison with
separation $|d_i - d_j|$ and forward pairs moving away from the refugium.  The
hypothesis predicts $r(S, d) < 0$ (sources near the refugium), $\Delta R^2 > 0$
and a forward-to-reverse slope ratio below one.

```{r arapat-tests-fn}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: [arapat-graph, arapat-axis]
membership <- igraph::components( beetles )$membership

component_of <- function( site ) {
  same <- membership == membership[nodes == site]
  igraph::induced_subgraph( beetles, nodes[same] )
}

test_expansion <- function( graph ) {
  dk  <- d[igraph::V( graph )$name]
  sep <- abs( outer( dk, dk, "-" ) )
  fwd <- outer( dk, dk, function( di, dj ) dj > di )
  list( gradient    = source_sink_test( graph, x = dk, nperm = 999 ),
        isolation   = ibgd( graph, distance = sep, nperm = 999 ),
        directional = ibgd( graph,
                            mode = "dcGD",
                            distance = sep,
                            forward = fwd ) )
}
```

**Southward expansion (central component).**  Site `93` lies in the central
group:

```{r arapat-south}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: arapat-tests-fn
set.seed( 2013 )
central <- component_of( "93" )
south   <- test_expansion( central )
south
```

Symmetric isolation by graph distance is absent here, but the directional
model recovers it: genetic distance accumulates moving north, toward the
refugium, and not moving south, away from it, the signature of a southward
expansion that averaging the two directions hides.  The source-sink scores
decline away from the refugium as predicted, but the gradient test does not
reject: the component is sparse, and its degree share is large (see the
diagnostics below).

**Northward expansion (northern component).**  Site `9` lies in the
northern group:

```{r arapat-north}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: arapat-tests-fn
set.seed( 2013 )
northern <- component_of( "9" )
north    <- test_expansion( northern )
north
```

Here symmetric isolation by distance is strong, and separate slopes do not
improve on it: distance accumulates at about the same rate in both directions.
With nine sites the source-sink test has little power, so this is weak
evidence about direction either way.

## Is the design adequate? Calibrating the tests

How often the directional tests point somewhere by chance depends on the
sampling design: the number of populations, the individuals in each, and the
loci.  `popgraph_diagnostics()` summarizes the design of the central component
and flags the common problems:

```{r arapat-diagnostics}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: arapat-south
central_sites <- igraph::V( central )$name
central_data  <- peninsula |>
  filter( Population %in% central_sites ) |>
  droplevels()

dg <- central_data |>
  popgraph_diagnostics( graph = central )
dg
```

Each check that has a threshold is marked `✓` or `!`, with a note saying what
a failed check means for the tests.  The same checks are available as a
data frame, and the per-population detail is in `dg$strata`:

```{r arapat-diagnostics-df}
as.data.frame( dg ) |>
  filter( status == "warn" ) |>
  select( check, value, note )
```

With five to ten beetles per site, every site falls below five expected
heterozygotes per locus, and the degree share is large: in such a graph a
population's score depends largely on how many neighbours it has, which is why
the gradient test above could not reject.  The calibrated isolation comparison
is the more reliable test here.

`popgraph_null()` calibrates it.  It simulates data sets with the component's
own sites, sample sizes, loci, alleles and missing genotypes under *symmetric*
migration (Wright-Fisher drift through a symmetric distance kernel, tuned to
the observed $G_{ST}$), rebuilds each Population Graph, and returns the null
distributions of $\Delta R^2$ and $r(S, x)$.  The 95th percentile of the null
$\Delta R^2$ replaces the rule $\Delta R^2 > 0$, and the fraction of null values
at or above the observed one is a one-sided $p$-value.  As for a published
analysis, 999 data sets are simulated:

```{r arapat-null}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: [arapat-south, arapat-diagnostics]
dk  <- d[central_sites]
sep <- abs( outer( dk, dk, "-" ) )
fwd <- outer( dk, dk, function( di, dj ) dj > di )

set.seed( 1 )
calibration <- central_data |>
  popgraph_null( axis = dk,
                 distance = sep,
                 forward = fwd,
                 graph = central,
                 nsim = 999 )
calibration
```

Under symmetric migration with this design, $\Delta R^2 > 0$ arises in a large
fraction of the null data sets, so the observed value alone would mean little;
against the calibrated cutoff, the southward expansion is significant.
Because the null depends on its migration model, check the cutoff's
sensitivity to `Ne`, `ngen` and the kernel (for example a two-dimensional,
great-circle `kernel_distance`).

### Designing a study

- **Individuals per population.**  Each edge is estimated from the variation
  *within* the populations it joins.  The allocation that is optimal for
  estimating differentiation (about $1/\Phi$ individuals per population;
  Falconer 1981, `optimal_sampling()`) is too thin for a Population Graph.
  Aim for roughly five expected heterozygotes per locus in each population
  ($n_i H_S \gtrsim 5$; about 30 individuals at moderate diversity); with ten,
  about half of simulated graphs fragment.
- **Populations.**  Once each is adequately sampled, more populations raise
  the power of the source-sink test.  With fewer than about ten, neither test
  establishes direction from one graph.
- **Loci and coverage.**  More loci raise the power of both tests, and sites
  should span the whole length of the hypothesized direction of flow.
- **Calibrate.**  These guidelines come from a one-dimensional simulation with
  two-allele loci; what carries over is calibrating with `popgraph_null()` for
  your own design.

Starting from the genotypes rather than a graph, `genetic_isolation()` builds
the graph and runs isolation by graph distance in one step, with the axis
given as a column:

```{r arapat-isolation}
#| eval: false
genetic_isolation( peninsula, mode = "IBGD", axis = "Latitude" )
genetic_isolation( peninsula, mode = "dcGD", axis = "Latitude" )
```

## Data quality: information loss

As loci fix, graphs are estimated from fewer informative loci, which inflates
$|\Delta|$ whatever the direction of gene flow.  `locus_subsample_null()`
rebuilds the graph from random subsets of polymorphic loci, to show how much
$|\Delta|$ information loss alone can produce at a given level of polymorphism:

```{r info-loss}
#| eval: false
arapat |>
  locus_subsample_null( k = c( 2, 3, 4, 6 ), nsub = 3 )
```

## Simulating directional gene flow

The `gravity` data come from an individual-based simulation of a directional
stepping stone.  @sec-simulation builds that simulation from scratch with
`make_populations()`, `migration_matrix( model = "stepping_stone_1d_asym" )`
and `simulate_pop()`, and follows the Population Graph and the source-sink
scores through a symmetric burn-in and three forward scenarios.

{{< include ../vignettes/children/genetic_gravity_nopipes.Rmd >}}

The *Araptus attenuatus* case study, calibration and data-quality steps:

```{r no-pipes-arapat}
#| eval: false
peninsula <- arapat[arapat$Species == "Peninsula", ]
n_site    <- table( peninsula$Population )
peninsula <- droplevels( peninsula[peninsula$Population %in%
                                     names( n_site )[n_site >= 4], ] )
beetles   <- population_graph( peninsula,
                               stratum = "Population",
                               decorate = TRUE )

coords <- strata_coordinates( peninsula, stratum = "Population" )
plot( gravity_field( beetles ),
      layout = coords,
      base = land_map,
      clip_to_base = TRUE,
      mask_dist = 0.6 )

central      <- component_of( "93" )
central_data <- droplevels(
  peninsula[peninsula$Population %in% igraph::V( central )$name, ]
)
dg <- popgraph_diagnostics( central_data,
                            stratum = "Population",
                            graph = central )
warn <- as.data.frame( dg )
warn[warn$status == "warn", c( "check", "value", "note" )]

calibration <- popgraph_null( central_data,
                              stratum = "Population",
                              axis = dk,
                              distance = sep,
                              forward = fwd,
                              graph = central,
                              nsim = 999 )

locus_subsample_null( arapat,
                      stratum = "Population",
                      k = c( 2, 3, 4, 6 ),
                      nsub = 3 )
```
